transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-held key because the delivered OLT TMS External API leaves no other option. It authenticates every request with a single global, company-scoped `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. So there is no user TMS credential to forward (Option A). re:cinq also can't exchange or hold a per-user credential, because none exists (Option B). Option C is the only one the published API supports. It keeps the key on the server (never from the browser or `ToolContext`) and enforces the boundary in Otto's own code. The boundary is Kristian's one non-negotiable requirement: customers can only see their own bookings. Identity comes from Clerk, where the organisation maps to the TMS `customerNumber`. Otto checks on each call which customer the request may ask about. A test checks that another customer's booking id returns an authorization error and no data. Because the key is company-scoped, user roles can't narrow what the TMS returns. Any role-based narrowing would have to be done in Otto's code, and the PoC doesn't do any.

judgements.reason: The answer says Otto uses a single global server-held key and enforces the customer boundary in its own code; it says forwarding is impossible because the TMS has no user-level auth, and that per-user credentials don't exist because the key is company-scoped, which matches the gold's one key per integration partner.
